title: Ishida Mitsunari's Three Cups of Tea
text:
A favorite Japanese legend tells how Ishida Mitsunari, later one of the most powerful administrators of 16th century Japan, first came to the notice of his lord. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, then governing the castle town of Nagahama in Omi province, was out hawking on a hot day. Thirsty, he stopped at a Buddhist temple and asked for tea. A boy serving at the temple, young Sakichi, brought it.

The first time, the boy brought a large bowl of lukewarm tea, which Hideyoshi drank down at once. He asked for another. This time the boy brought a smaller cup of hotter tea. When Hideyoshi asked for a third, the boy brought a small cup of very hot, strong tea, to be sipped and savored.

Hideyoshi understood what the boy had done. He had judged the needs of a parched man first, then of a man whose thirst was eased, then of a man who could enjoy the tea. Impressed by such attention, Hideyoshi took the boy into his service. As Ishida Mitsunari he rose to become one of Hideyoshi's most trusted officials.
lesson: Pay attention to what the other person actually needs at this moment, not what is easiest for you to give. That kind of care is noticed.
source: Edo-period anecdote collections about Toyotomi Hideyoshi and his retainers
caveat: The story is a legend with no contemporary evidence, and it is told with variations.
